Siemens Energy: a contracted earnings step-up to FY2028, priced as if the cycle had already turned

Prepared 7 November 2026 for Richard. Share price €118.68 (25 October 2026, the price used in the model). Siemens Energy reports FY2026 results, FY2027 guidance and new FY2030 targets on 11 November 2026, four days from now. Definitions, bases and sources are in the end notes.

#0Summary: the case in one page

The bottom line

Siemens Energy offers an earnings-driven return of about +39% to December 2027 at a below-median multiple, with a cushioned downside. The model reaches that return at the guideline multiple of 15.47x, barely above today's multiple, so the return needs no re-rating. Even at the ten-year "crash" multiple of 11.2x, the value per share at end-2027 is about €120, which is today's price.

  • Why the skew is positive: the market is pricing an order peak whose earnings effect arrives only in FY2030, while about four-fifths of the earnings step to FY2028 is already contracted or demonstrated.
  • Where we are more cautious than the market: cash, where our free cash flow is €0.9bn to €1.1bn a year below consensus in FY2027 to FY2028, and margins in FY2029 to FY2030.
  • The decisive date: 11 November 2026, when the FY2030 target, the buyback pace and the cash guide decide whether the multiple becomes company-driven again.

The case: about four-fifths of the earnings step to FY2028 rests on facts already demonstrated. Siemens Energy is converting a €162bn backlog, booked at prices 20% or more above the contracts it replaces, through factories whose new capacity is already being installed. That conversion lifts the margin from 6% in FY2025 to about 12% in FY2026, 15% in FY2027 and 16.5% in FY2028, and lifts adjusted EPS from €1.63 to €4.6, €6.5 and €8.4. Four demonstrated elements carry most of the step: contracted volume (87% of FY2027 revenue is already in the backlog), booked price, segment margins already at the FY2028 targets (Grid 19.9% and Gas Services 17.3% in Q3 FY2026), and a capacity ramp that is half delivered. The remaining fifth depends on execution: shipping 50 large gas turbines in FY2027 through a casting and labour supply chain that the company does not control, and keeping wind at a small profit after two incidents on its offshore platform in Taiwan this autumn.

Why the shares have fallen: about two-thirds is the sector, one-third the company. The share price is down 38% from its April high and 32% in six months, while FY2027 consensus EPS rose 11% over the same six months. The 24-month-forward P/E has therefore fallen from 27x to about 14.4x, the 32nd percentile of the stock's own history and inside its "conservative" band. About two-thirds of the fall in the multiple comes from the de-rating of the AI-power cohort in a risk-off market with a 5.1% US 10-year yield: the stock now moves with a beta of 1.5 to its peer basket, and the basket explains 62% of the stock's daily variance. About one-third is specific to Siemens Energy: the "peak orders" fear after gas orders rose 61% in Q3, the pricing gap to GE Vernova, and wind. The market is therefore pricing today a risk whose earnings effect arrives only in FY2030: orders peaking, and competitors' new capacity landing in 2028 to 2030.

The eight things that matter most.

  1. Earnings to FY2028 are unusually predictable; cash and the multiple are not. The FY2027 EBITA range is about ±7% around €7.3bn, with the most likely outcome above the base case. The FY2027 free cash flow range is ±27%. The 18-month share-price range is about -35% to +65%, and the multiple sets almost all of it.
  2. Cash peaks in FY2026, while profit keeps rising to FY2030. Contract liabilities (customer prepayments) reached €28.1bn in June 2026, up €5.4bn in nine months. As orders normalise, the prepayment pool stops growing in FY2027 and gives back about €3.5bn over FY2028 to FY2030. Our free cash flow is therefore €0.9bn to €1.1bn a year below FactSet consensus in FY2027 to FY2028 on a like-for-like basis, and cash is the one place where our view and the market narrative will collide within the next 18 months. One caveat: the company's own compiled consensus (4 November) shows FY2027 pre-tax free cash flow of only €5.5bn, far below FactSet's figure, so part of the sell-side may already be at our level.
  3. FY2027 guidance is a floor and will probably be raised, but the FY2030 target will be set above our forecast. We put a 60% probability on at least one raise to FY2027 guidance by August 2027, and a 65% probability on a FY2030 group margin target of 20% or above. Our FY2030 margin is 18.4%, or about 18.9% excluding Transformation of Industry. The short-dated guidance cushion is real; the long-dated cushion is about to be used up.
  4. Our FY2027 and FY2028 EPS match consensus (€6.54 against €6.32; €8.36 against €8.35), but we build them differently. We forecast 2% to 3% less revenue (wind flat, grid limited by capacity) and slightly higher margins. Our estimates therefore give no earnings edge in either direction for 18 months; our edge is negative on cash and positive on the multiple.
  5. Two binary inputs decide whether FY2028 EPS lands above or below our base case, and the 11 November results and the December annual report should resolve both. The first input is whether the Siemens brand fee of roughly €400m a year stops as group entities rebrand to Omterra during FY2027 to FY2028. Our €250m saving for FY2028 is the expected value of a two-outcome distribution, and the two outcomes differ by about 4% of FY2028 EPS. The second input is whether the buyback steps up to €3bn a year, which is worth about 1% of EPS.
  6. The negative tails are few and discrete, and each is larger than the continuous upside. They are a systemic finding on the SG 14 offshore wind platform (about 12% probability; €1bn to €2bn), a two-quarter slip in the large-turbine ramp (about 15%; 4% to 5% of FY2027 EBITA deferred), a deferral of data-centre deliveries (10% to 15%; small for EPS, €2bn to €4bn for cash), and organisational overload in 2027 (a carve-out, the rebrand, India and two capacity ramps, while the contracts of the CFO and the Grid head end in November 2027). Their combined probability is perhaps one in three, so the probability-weighted mean outcome sits a little below the most likely outcome.
  7. The de-rating has largely happened; the estimate cuts have not. At the ten-year "crash" multiple of 11.2x on the forward EPS the model expects at end-2027 (about €10.7), the share price would be about €120, which is today's price. A bear case therefore needs both a lower multiple and lower earnings: a 15% EPS cut at 11.2x gives about €100, or -15%.
  8. The return at the guideline multiple comes from earnings, not from a re-rating. At 15.47x (the 40th percentile of the stock's history, and the Phases guideline for a Stalling stock), which is barely above today's multiple, the model gives +39% to December 2027 and +67% to June 2029 (21% a year), almost all from EPS rolling forward. A re-rating to the ten-year median would add about 9 points. The bull case, at the two-year median of 22.5x, would add about 45 points, and it needs the whole sector cohort to re-rate, not just the company.
Downside anchor At the ten-year crash multiple of 11.2x on the forward EPS expected at end-2027 (about €10.7), the share is worth about €120: today's price. A bear case needs both a lower multiple and lower earnings.
11 November 2026 The FY2026 results, the FY2027 guide and the FY2030 targets will resolve the two binary inputs (the brand-fee stop date and the buyback pace) and will set consensus for FY2029 to FY2030.

Where we differ from the market: we agree on near-term earnings, and differ on cash, the later margins and the multiple. We are more cautious than consensus on cash in FY2027 to FY2028 and on margins in FY2029 to FY2030, because we expect prices on new orders to erode from 2028 rather than plateau. We are more constructive than the market on the multiple, because the peak-orders risk is three years from the income statement and a 14x multiple already reflects it. The setup is therefore a "Demand-driven EPS step-up, with a large corporate-change overlay, on a Stalling multiple", not a clean one: a strong, forecastable earnings engine wrapped in a question about the quality of cash and a multiple driven by the sector cohort.

#1Operating environment: tailwinds and headwinds

Conclusion: the external tailwinds are among the strongest in European capital goods and are contracted for two to five years, but the growth rate of demand is starting to slow and the market regime is hostile to the multiple, so over the next six months the tailwinds will help earnings far more than they help the share price.

Three demand drivers are accelerating at once, and they compound one another. The first driver is load growth from AI and electrification: data centres are a distinct 40 GW pillar of gas demand and account for half of North American gas orders, and US utility generation capex is up 36% year on year. The second driver is the grid replacement and reinforcement cycle: over 1,500 GW of projects wait in grid-connection queues, the EU has a €584bn grid plan, and the company itself expects a 10% shortfall in transformer supply to persist in 2030. The third driver is the switch from coal to gas.

Orders confirm the demand, and the quality of reservations is now proven. Of the 15 GW of gas orders booked in Q3, 12 GW converted from reservation agreements, which shows that reservations do turn into firm orders.

Regulation is net positive for gas and grid. The EU ban on SF6 (sulphur hexafluoride, an insulating gas used in switchgear) is legislated and dated: it applies to medium voltage from 2026 and to 52 to 145 kV equipment from 2028. National Grid has approved only three SF6-free suppliers, and Siemens Energy is one of them. In the US, an executive order excludes equipment of 69 kV and above from vendors tied to 24 countries; the Department of Energy's rules are due on 24 December, and the order lengthens the period in which US grid prices stay high.

Four headwinds are real, and the most important is that demand growth is slowing.

The environment is unusually favourable for operations and unusually hostile for the valuation, and the two effects must be analysed separately. Supply is limited by capacity until 2028 to 2030, so load growth converts into higher prices, not only into higher volume. Even Morgan Stanley's 2027 bear case, in which global gas orders halve to 50 GW, shortens the backlog's duration and weakens prepayments but barely touches gas revenue in FY2027 to FY2029.

Demand risk should be modelled where it bites: first in the multiple, second in cash, and third in pricing from FY2029. Cash is hit because prepayments stop growing. Demand poses close to no risk to FY2027 revenue. Input-cost risk is mostly passed on to customers through indexation, 95% local sourcing, 75% to 100% hedging and, in grid, back-to-back escalation clauses tied to metal indices. The residual exposure is on short-cycle products, a three- to six-month lag in indexation, and India.

Where we differ from the market: a 2026 order peak matters for cash and the multiple, not for earnings to FY2029. The market's debate is whether 2026 is the order peak, and the market treats a "yes" as negative for the stock now. We agree that 2026 is probably the peak for gas orders. Two external questions are under-discussed, and the sell-side research on Siemens Energy addresses neither: whether behind-the-meter gas generation for data centres is a bridge or a permanent solution (a 2027 question), and whether US electricity-affordability politics will drive Siemens Energy's grid orders.

Counter-case: a hyperscaler capex pause could turn reservations into deferrals. Data-centre developers hold 24% of the turbine backlog, and credit stress could push hyperscalers to pause their capex. Morgan Stanley's stress test puts a 50% delay in 2028 data-centre deliveries at about €1bn of revenue and €0.3bn of EBITA (about 3%). Separately, the affordability backlash could slow US grid orders from FY2027.

What would change our view: Gas Services book-to-bill below 1.0, management's gas market view cut below 100 GW, grid book-to-bill below 1.2, or a quarterly working-capital outflow above €1bn.

Score: 87, set by the Rater. AI and electrification load, the grid replacement cycle and coal-to-gas switching reach gas and grid (about 87% of profit) through a contracted, capacity-bound three-player market where demand converts into price (gas like-for-like +20%), backed by dated regulation (EU SF6 phase-out, National Grid's three approved suppliers, the US 69 kV fence); consensus sales and EPS growth sit at the 91st percentile and tell the truth here because 87% of FY2027 revenue is in a EUR 162bn backlog. Wind (24% of revenue, Chinese price competition, US offshore dead), input-cost inflation largely passed through and a turning second derivative of orders trim it, so it sits just above Arteche's grid-only tailwind and below Indra's, coherent with the group's 80 but higher because the forces are contracted for two to five years and reach most of the business as it will be after the Transformation of Industry sale.

#2Internally driven corporate change

Conclusion: the internal change is strong, broad and well funded, and it acts on margin, growth, capital and the multiple at once; wind remains inside the group, and the execution load of 2027 is the main problem.

The same management team has turned a state-rescued conglomerate into what it calls a "disciplined execution machine". CEO Christian Bruch (in post since 2020, contract extended to April 2030) and CFO Maria Ferraro (contract to November 2027) led the company from a state rescue in 2023 to about €8bn of net cash. They pulled five sets of levers:

  • Pricing and selectivity over volume: reservation fees, escalation clauses, limits on liability for consequential loss, and data-centre orders accepted only for permitted sites.
  • Brownfield productivity over greenfield capacity: large gas turbine output rises from 35 to 50 units in FY2027; medium units have already risen from 50 to about 80 and head toward 100 by FY2028; transformer and switchgear capacity rises 50% by 2030 on €6bn of capex.
  • Portfolio simplification: Transformation of Industry (€5.7bn of revenue, 17,000 staff) is being legally separated, with a decision due by mid-2027 and private equity bids above €10bn; the Omterra rebrand from late 2026 ends the Siemens brand fee; and a 51% controlling stake in Siemens Energy India follows by June 2028 for about €4.5bn.
  • Capital returns from a standing start: the dividend has restarted, about €3bn of a €6bn buyback was done in FY2026, and a step-up to about €3bn a year is expected on 11 November.
  • Governance: Siemens AG's stake is down to about 10% with one board seat, and an activist investor, Ananym, is pushing for a spin-off of wind.

The changes act on all four value levers at once, and customers and earnings fund them, not debt. The four levers are margin (pricing, the wind repair, the end of the brand royalty, portfolio mix), growth (capacity), capital (buybacks) and the multiple (simplification, and better comparability with GE Vernova). Customer prepayments and the earnings step-up provide the funding. The Transformation of Industry separation is the activist's first win, and that win raises the odds of a decision on the larger perimeter question, wind, in 2027 to 2028, once the onshore business stabilises.

The main problems: wind stays inside the group, and 2027 stacks five demanding programmes on one management team. Wind is being fixed, not exited, so a near-zero-margin business with a long warranty tail (24% of revenue) stays inside the group for at least 18 more months. The 2027 calendar stacks a 17,000-person carve-out, a rebrand of thousands of legal entities, the India step and two capacity ramps, under a CFO and a Grid head whose contracts end on 30 November 2027. The carve-out is already contested: the supervisory board and the works council rejected the June spin-off proposal, which forced the pivot to a sale.

Pay governance, customer goodwill and capital allocation are weak spots. Pay governance leans towards management: variable pay can scale to 400% in the first year after the guaranteed period, and the 2022 and 2023 incentive targets were reset retroactively. Customers describe the company as "transactional", and that loss of goodwill will cost the company when capacity frees up after 2028. Capital allocation does not respond to the share price: the company bought the second buyback tranche at an average of €154.63, against €118.68 today, and it is buying the India stake from the former parent's sphere at a full price.

The self-help items support FY2027 to FY2028 margins in the upper half of the guided ranges; the 2027 execution load is the main risk. Formal guidance has been a floor for two clean years. The mechanical self-help items (the royalty removal, the mix uplift from the Transformation of Industry exit, interest income, and the run-off of legacy wind contracts) argue for leaning FY2027 to FY2028 margins toward the upper half of the ranges. The 2027 execution load is the clearest strength the company has still to acquire, and the kind of weakness that stays least visible in the numbers until it fails.

Where we differ from the market: the market prices the record and the portfolio steps, but not three risks. The market credits management with the beat-and-raise record and prices the portfolio steps (the buyback step-up and a Transformation of Industry value of €11bn to €13bn). The market does not price three things: the strain on management bandwidth in 2027; the mid-FY2027 restatement of Transformation of Industry to discontinued operations, which will break the comparability of consensus for a quarter or two and raise the reported margin by 0.1 to 0.3 points; and the two-outcome timing of the royalty saving.

Counter-case: part of the record is the cycle. Seven of eleven energy contractors beat and raised guidance in the same months. The only downturn test in this management team's record, wind in 2022 to 2023, was failed. Management itself calls a wind exit "political".

What would change our view: a Transformation of Industry signing at €11bn or more with the proceeds returned, or a decision to separate wind, would make the case cleaner and the multiple company-driven again. A CFO departure without orderly succession, or a second works-council defeat on the carve-out, would turn the bandwidth risk from latent to live.

Score: 84, set by the Rater. A broad, funded programme already in earnings and aimed at growth as well as repair: pricing and selectivity discipline, brownfield capacity (large turbines 35 to 50, transformers +50%), the Transformation of Industry sale (bids above EUR 10bn), the rebrand ending a roughly EUR 400m royalty, the India control step, the dividend restart and a EUR 6bn buyback, all funded by prepayments and net cash of about EUR 8bn; the margin move from -9% to 12% in three years is real though much of it is external price (counted in topic 1). Wind fixed rather than exited, a stacked 2027 agenda under a CFO and Grid head whose contracts end in November 2027, management-friendly pay and pro-cyclical buybacks keep it off 90, in line with the group's 83 and above Arteche's 81 for its larger scope.

#3Industry structure, business model, financial profile, management

Conclusion: gas and grid sit in an excellent, concentrated, barrier-protected industry structure, with a service annuity underneath and a capacity-scarcity window on top, and they are run by a management team proven in those two businesses; wind, customer goodwill and prepayment-flattered returns are the weak points, and they are where the foundations will be tested after 2028.

In gas and grid, which earn about 87% of profit, the industry structure is as supportive as capital goods gets. Gas turbines are a three-player oligopoly with about 85% market share. Siemens Energy is number two or three, a few points behind Mitsubishi Heavy Industries and GE Vernova, and it took 42% of orders for turbines above 100 MW in Q3. High-voltage direct current (HVDC) transmission has three or four Western suppliers, and Siemens Energy holds about 30%. Prequalification and reference fleets are barriers to entry, capacity is sold out, and customers pay for delivery dates.

Transformers are the contestable piece, and wind is the opposite of gas and grid. Korean makers hold 19% of US transformer imports, and customers see Hitachi as faster and cheaper; the new US fence on vendors now protects the US transformer market too. In wind, Chinese makers are 20% to 40% cheaper, Nordex holds 48% of European onshore, and Vestas is regaining offshore share with its V236 turbine.

Competitors put margin first today, but they are cyclical by nature. In the last gas downcycle (2016 to 2020), prices fell one to two years after volume, and the margin of Siemens Power and Gas fell from 16% to about 5%.

The durable moats are the service annuity and the technology; the moat behind today's excess margin, capacity scarcity, has a visible expiry date. The durable moats are the installed-base service annuity (17-year agreements with an attach rate above 70%; Deutsche Bank estimates that 160 GW of additions by 2030 could add €3.6bn of annual service revenue within the decade), hot-section casting technology with in-house integration of blades and vanes, prequalification (SF6-free products; approvals from transmission operators), and HVDC scale. Capacity scarcity, by contrast, is a first-mover window: GE Vernova expands to 30 GW of gas capacity by 2030, Hitachi's Mississippi plant opens in 2029, and Mitsubishi adds 30% by FY2028. About half of current gas and grid pricing is scarcity rent; the other half is cost pass-through and a technology premium.

Durable moats
Installed-base service annuity (17-year agreements, over 70% attach); hot-section casting and blade integration; prequalification; HVDC scale
Expiring window
Capacity scarcity: about half of today's gas and grid pricing is scarcity rent, fading as GE Vernova, Hitachi and Mitsubishi add capacity in 2028 to 2030

The financial profile has been transformed, but two forms of over-earning must be discounted. Group return on invested capital moved from -4% in FY2024 to very high levels (Grid earned 52% in FY2024, before the latest repricing). Returns are high because customers fund working capital (contract liabilities equal about half of revenue), reported capital employed is small, and there is no financial gearing: net cash is about €8bn, the credit rating is Baa1, and the company has a €9bn guarantee facility and a €4bn undrawn revolving credit facility. The first over-earning is that prepayments inflate free cash flow and returns, and both reverse if book-to-bill falls below 1. The second is that part of the margin is scarcity rent, which fades on new orders from about 2028.

Consensus EPS growth of 40% in FY2027 and 32% in FY2028 is far above large peers' growth, and Siemens Energy achieves it with capex of only 4% to 5% of revenue and no leverage.

Management's record splits cleanly: outstanding in gas, grid and cash since FY2024, and poor where quality and capital allocation were tested. Since FY2024 the team has beaten every FY2025 target, delivered free cash flow 370% above the original guide, and raised FY2026 guidance twice. Earlier, the 2022 buyout of Siemens Gamesa's minority shareholders preceded the June 2023 wind quality crisis and a €4.6bn loss in FY2023. Management's ambition is high on margin and returns (toward 20% by FY2030, from -9% in FY2023) and deliberately moderate on volume (no greenfield gas capacity). The culture is improving but not yet unified: a German industrial heritage with co-determination (Spanish wind job cuts were negotiated down from 423 to 255) sits alongside a Danish-Spanish wind arm.

The earnings step to FY2028 is predictable because mechanical forces drive it, not new competitive wins. The mechanical forces are backlog repricing, service growth, the run-off of loss-making wind contracts, the royalty saving and mix. The competitive advantages are weakest exactly where they would matter in a downturn: in customer goodwill (value has been extracted from customers, not shared with them), in price leadership against GE Vernova (Siemens Energy prices at $572/kW against GE Vernova's $800/kW, and GE Vernova's gas backlog margin rose 1,100bps in 2025 against Siemens Energy's 500bps), and in onshore wind.

Where we differ from the market: the discount to GE Vernova is partly deserved and partly closable. The market values Siemens Energy at a 45% EV/EBITA discount to GE Vernova. The market pays for the diffuse, short-cycle drivers of ABB and Schneider (at the 73rd and 77th percentiles of their own multiple histories), while it discounts the contracted-margin cohort (Siemens Energy, the cable makers, Legrand) to the bottom third. We think the discount to GE Vernova is partly deserved (wind, US share, pricing) and partly closable through delivery and portfolio events. The cohort discount is a fair price for concentrated drivers, and it is the right reason to accept a mid-range fair multiple for Siemens Energy rather than a compounder's multiple.

Counter-case: scale did not prevent the wind quality failure. The organisation was slow to detect the wind platform's defects. R&D intensity is falling (from 3.5% to 3.1% of revenue), which is efficient now and a risk in the long term.

What would change our view: evidence that scarcity rents are eroding before 2028 (for example, new-order margins below backlog margins reported at a pre-close call), or GE Vernova changing its pricing behaviour when its new capacity lands.

Score: 70, set by the Rater. Gas and grid sit in a concentrated, prequalification-gated oligopoly with a 17-year service annuity, hot-section casting know-how and HVDC scale, but Siemens Energy is number two or three, about half of today's pricing is scarcity rent with a visible expiry from 2028, a quarter of revenue is a weak-franchise wind business, customer goodwill has been spent and management's strong record since FY2024 sits on the Gamesa error. The figures (ROIC 11% at the 71st percentile, operating margin at the 19th, FCF/net income at the 91st) understate the forward margin but overstate durable returns, which are flattered by prepayments and depend on low-predictability post-2028 pricing, so it sits just above Volex, coherent with groups of 60 to 70.

#4Conservatism of guidance; record of delivery and upgrades

Conclusion: current guidance is conservative and will probably be raised at least once by August 2027, and the record since FY2024 is a consistent beat-and-raise in gas, grid and cash; the FY2030 target, however, is about to be set at or above our forecast, so the guidance cushion is short-dated.

Since FY2024 the pattern has been consistent: a low initial guide, a raise after results once evidence supports it, and delivery well above the top of the range. The chart below shows the FY2025 record and the progress against the FY2028 segment targets. In FY2026, management raised margin guidance to 10% to 12% at Q2 and narrowed it to the upper end at Q3, and raised pre-tax cash guidance from €4bn to €5bn to about €8bn, of which the company had already generated €7.16bn in nine months.

The FY2028 targets set at the November 2025 Capital Markets Day are being reached two years early. The targets were a group margin of 14% to 16%, 18% to 20% each for Gas Services and Grid, and 3% to 5% for wind. Grid reached its range in Q3 FY2026 and Gas Services nearly did, and Deutsche Bank reports that the group range is being pulled forward to FY2027. Consensus FY2028 margin (16.3%) already sits above the top of the formal range, so the sell-side stopped using guidance as its central case a year ago. Sell-side FY2027 EPS has risen 47% over twelve months, and the dashboard rates sell-side earnings momentum A.

The CFO's style is explicitly conservative, and the company uses pre-close calls to steer consensus. At the 30 September pre-close call (the previous one was on 30 June), management confirmed that new orders carry "substantially higher margins" than both the executed backlog and the orders signed in early FY2026.

Formal guidance is a floor, and a raise to the FY2027 guide is five times likelier than a cut. The initial FY2027 guide on 11 November is likely to be set below what the backlog supports: we put a 75% probability on the guided midpoint sitting below our 14.7% margin, either through a 13% to 15% range or through the 14% to 16% FY2028 range pulled forward. We put the probability of at least one raise at Q2 (May 2027, the habitual raise point) or Q3 (August 2027) at about 60%, the probability of meeting the top of the range without a raise at 28%, and the probability of a cut at 12%. The FY2026 guide will be met on margin and probably beaten on cash: the €8bn guide implies only €0.84bn in Q4, which leaves €0.5bn to €1bn of upside.

The FY2030 target is a different matter: the long-dated guidance cushion is about to be spent. Management will set the FY2030 target with the Transformation of Industry exit and the royalty removal in view. We put a 65% probability on a target of 20% or above; Morgan Stanley expects 20% to 22%, Deutsche Bank expects 20% rising to 22% with portfolio effects, and consensus is 19.8%. On our model, a 20% margin on the current perimeter needs gas and grid pricing to hold on orders booked in 2027 to 2028, which we do not assume. The next genuinely conservative marker will therefore be the FY2028 guide in November 2027, not the FY2030 target.

Short-dated cushion: intact
75% probability the FY2027 guide midpoint sits below our 14.7% margin; habitual raise points May and August 2027.
Long-dated cushion: about to be spent
65% probability the FY2030 target is 20% or above, against our 18.4% and consensus 19.8%.

Where we differ from the market: the FY2030 target and the cash guide carry more risk than the market expects. The market expects the raise pattern to continue and treats the FY2030 target as a positive catalyst. We agree that FY2027 guidance will be raised. We think a FY2030 target of 20% or more is as much a statement about the perimeter and self-help as about pricing, and that over three years the target is more likely to be met with difficulty or trimmed (40%) than raised (15%). The cash guide is the trap inside the 11 November event. A FY2027 pre-tax cash guide of "€6bn to €7bn" would be conservative by the company's habits and consistent with our model, yet the bear narrative would still read it as the prepayment loop turning; we see about a 40% chance that the market reads the cash guide negatively on the day.

Counter-case: two clean years is a short record. FY2021 to FY2023 brought repeated profit warnings and a withdrawn guide. The recent beats came during a sector-wide wave of beats and raises. The only misses in the latest results were in orders (grid and wind), and orders are where the next disappointment is most likely.

What would change our view: a FY2027 margin guide of 15% or above, which would leave no cushion, or a FY2030 target below 20%, which would be realistic on our numbers but would disappoint a buy-side whose expectations sit above the sell-side's.

Score: 80, set by the Rater. Since FY2024 the company has guided low and beaten the top of the range: FY2025 revenue guidance raised twice and beaten, margin 6.0% against 3% to 5%, FCF EUR 4.7bn against up to EUR 1bn; FY2026 raised twice; CMD FY2028 segment targets reached two years early; and the FY2027 guide is likely set below what the backlog supports (75% probability). Held back from the 80s because the clean record is only two to three years after the FY2021-23 warnings, partly sector-wide, and consensus already sits above the FY2028 range with the FY2030 cushion about to be spent; above the guidance group's 73 because the delivery itself is exceptional.

#5Revenue to profit: pricing power, operating leverage, cost-out, feedback loops

Conclusion: the business converts revenue growth into profit growth roughly three times as fast through contracted price and backlog volume; operating leverage is the smaller and reversible part, and the prepayment loop is already turning from a cash tailwind into a cash headwind.

Pricing power is the main profit engine, and it is applied, not conjectured. The tiles below show the price gains in gas and grid. In addition, the grid backlog margin rises about 300bps a year, and service contracts are indexed 80% to factory prices and 20% to wages, with commodity adjusters that move only upward. Book-to-bill stayed far above 1 through the price rises, so the higher prices have done little to deter customers so far.

Price adds far more to revenue growth than to margin, because much of the price increase only matches cost increases. Realised price adds about 5 points to revenue growth in FY2027 and 4.5 points in FY2028, but only about 0.8 to 1.0 points a year to the group margin net of cost inflation. Management describes pricing as "plateauing on a high level": the price rises are done, but the earnings rise from them is not, because the backlog converts into revenue over two to four years.

Operating leverage is the smaller profit engine and the more reversible one. Of the €3.8bn EBITA increase from FY2026 to FY2028, about half is volume on the backlog at today's margins. About one-third is price and mix already contracted, plus fixed-cost absorption (SG&A falls from 8.9% to about 8.0% of revenue, better than the 8.7% target, and R&D from 2.9% to 2.4%). About one-sixth is self-help (wind from breakeven to €0.37bn, and the royalty saving). Only about €0.5bn to €0.7bn of the fixed-cost absorption would reverse quickly in a downturn. Incremental margins run at 28% to 34%, below Q3's 42% excluding wind, because new capacity brings new depreciation and ramp-up inefficiency.

Financial leverage adds little: with no debt, EPS gains only from buybacks and interest income. Buybacks, net of the interest forgone on the cash spent, add about 1% to 1.5% to EPS a year, as the share count falls from 845m to 802m by FY2028 and to about 768m by FY2030. Net financial items swing from -€293m to a small positive figure (guarantee fees disappear and €11bn of cash earns interest), a one-off gain of about €0.30 of EPS.

Cost-out is a secondary driver. Savings against FY2026 are about €0.25bn in FY2027 and €0.65bn by FY2028, mainly from the royalty and overhead leverage. Wind cost-out (€300m of integration savings; onshore factories cut from 10 to 4) is largely done and now shows up as fixed-cost absorption.

Three reinforcing loops carry profit, but the prepayment loop has already turned in cash terms. The first reinforcing loop, backlog repricing, fades from FY2029. The second, the installed-base service annuity, strengthens after FY2029 as FY2026 to FY2028 deliveries enter service, and it sets the margin floor beyond 2030. The third, a fragile wind loop, lifts the margin through selectivity on flat volume, but a serial quality issue would reverse it at once. The prepayment loop works the other way for cash: working capital contributes +€3.6bn in FY2026 (probably conservative against €5.4bn of contract-liability inflow in nine months) and +€1.0bn in FY2027, then -€0.8bn, -€1.5bn and -€1.2bn in FY2028 to FY2030. Three balancing loops (competitor capacity, customer goodwill and US affordability politics) act on new-order prices from about 2028 and on reported margins from about FY2030, and because the three are correlated they do not offset one another.

Profit keeps rising to FY2028 while cash has already peaked: our free cash flow is €0.9bn to €1.1bn a year below FactSet consensus in FY2027 to FY2028, like for like.

Revenue growth of 12% to 13% becomes EBITA growth of 36% (FY2027) and 26% (FY2028), and EPS growth of 43% and 28%. The conversion is contractual and visible, which is the best kind of conversion. Siemens Energy is, however, a priced-backlog machine, not a pricing-power franchise: when the scarcity of factory slots ends, roughly half of the price gain on new orders is at risk, with a one- to two-year lag.

Where we differ from the market: the market under-weights the gap in timing between profit and cash. Consensus incremental margins (30% to 36%) match ours. The market, however, under-weights the fact that profit keeps rising to FY2028 while cash has already peaked. Morgan Stanley calls pricing stabilisation the "next thing to digest"; our FY2029 to FY2030 base case has prices eroding on new orders.

Counter-case: the grid price-cost balance could squeeze FY2028 to FY2029 deliveries, although the evidence on indexation says the near-term risk is low. Indian transformer prices per MVA are flat while copper is up 40% to 50%. We allow for that squeeze with a Grid margin that rises only 0.7 points from FY2027 to FY2028. The evidence on indexation (back-to-back metal escalators; Hitachi with 70% of orders on flexible pricing; HD Hyundai Electric passing through 84% of tariff costs) says the near-term risk is lower than first feared, and the residual risk to the FY2027 grid margin is skewed upward.

What would change our view: new-order margins reported below executed-backlog margins at a pre-close call, or a quarterly working-capital outflow above €1bn before FY2028.

Score: 76, set by the Rater. Pricing is applied and contracted (gas +20% like-for-like, grid +10-12% a year, services indexed) and the backlog repricing and installed-base service loops are real, so revenue growth of 12-13% gives EBITA growth of 36% and 26% and EPS growth of 43% and 28% (about three times revenue, well above the Universe's two). It stops at strong-on-two-elements because financial leverage is nil, cost-out is secondary, incremental margins of 28-34% include new depreciation, and the memo itself calls it a priced-backlog machine whose pricing is proven only in a scarcity cycle, with about half the new-order price gain at risk when slots free up.

#6Forecast financials: scope for double-digit growth and higher margins than the past

Conclusion: double-digit revenue growth to FY2029 and a margin three times the company's best year are the base case and are well underpinned to FY2028; our numbers are at consensus on earnings and below consensus on cash and on the FY2029 to FY2030 slope.

The base case: the margin triples and adjusted EPS rises about sevenfold by FY2030.

Against the past, every line steps up. Revenue growth roughly doubles, to about 11% a year to FY2030, against 7.3% a year in FY2020 to FY2025 and 5.2% from FY2019. The margin triples from its best-ever 6.0%. EPS rises about sevenfold. Free cash flow after tax and leases settles at €5bn to €7bn a year, against €0.2bn to €1.0bn in FY2019 to FY2024 and a cyclical peak of €6.9bn in FY2026.

Against consensus, we match on earnings and sit below on revenue and cash. Our EBITA is in line for FY2027 and FY2028 (-0.5% and -1.8%), while our revenue is 2% to 3% lower. Our FY2027 EPS is 3.5% higher, mostly for definitional reasons: the consensus median mixes adjusted and reported definitions, and our tax rate is 1 to 2 points lower. Our FY2028 EPS is in line. Our FY2029 EBITA is 6.7% below the consensus of the six brokers who forecast that year. Our free cash flow is €0.9bn to €1.1bn a year lower in FY2027 to FY2028 like for like, and €1.3bn to €1.6bn lower as printed, because FactSet's figure does not deduct about €0.45bn of lease payments. Our capex is above consensus (€2.2bn to €2.3bn against €1.9bn to €2.1bn) because grid capacity rises 50% to 2030.

The step to FY2028 is the most forecastable earnings growth the company has had, so the real question is the slope after FY2028. Volume is contracted, price is booked, and segment margins are already at target. The FY2027 EBITA range is about €6.8bn to €7.8bn (±7%), with the most likely outcome above the base; the FY2028 range is about €8.1bn to €10.3bn (±12%) and balanced. The cash range is three to four times wider (€4.0bn to €7.0bn in FY2027). The scope for higher growth and margins than in the past is therefore not in doubt for four years. After FY2028, our margins of 17.6% and 18.4% sit below the 20% that the market expects management to target.

Over the next 18 months, revenue growth stays above 10% in every quarter. Q4 FY2026 profit before special items should be about €1.41bn (an 11.4% margin), below Q3's 14.2%, because Q3 carried one-off gains and Q4 is seasonally weaker. Q1 FY2027 benefits from an easy comparison with the prior year's dollar exchange rate. The model's own Q4 FY2026 margin of about 17% is on a different basis and must not be compared with the 11 November print.

Where we differ from the market: at the median on EPS, and below on cash, revenue and the later margins. On FY2027 to FY2028 EPS we are at the consensus median. We are below consensus on cash. We are below on FY2029 to FY2030, because we model price erosion on new orders rather than a plateau, and a Grid margin path slower than the backlog's run-rate. We are below on revenue, because we keep wind flat (consensus has growth of 3.7% a year), keep grid limited by capacity, and assume no benefit from currency translation.

Counter-case to our base: the company's own compiled consensus is higher on FY2027 segment margins. The pre-event consensus that the company compiled on 4 November has FY2027 Grid at 20.8% and Gas Services at 18.4%, against our 19.3% and 18.7%, and revenue growth of 14.4% against our 13.0%. Morgan Stanley has FY2027 EBITA at €7.8bn (a 15.6% margin). If Grid holds its Q3 run-rate, FY2027 EBITA is nearer €7.6bn to €7.8bn, which is the upper half of our range.

What would change our view: the 11 November guide and FY2030 framework (buyback pace, royalty treatment, Transformation of Industry perimeter), the Q1 FY2027 shipment count for large turbines, or a root-cause finding on the Taiwan incidents.

Score: 94, set by the Rater. About 25-26% a year sits well inside the 15-30% A band and the margin path triples the best year before FY2026 (6.0% to 18.4%), almost entirely organic (India is near EPS-neutral after minorities), so it sits high in the band; held off the top because the growth is front-loaded (43%, 28%, then about 20% and 15%) and the FY2029-30 slope rests on new-order pricing the memo sees eroding.

#7Scope for upgrades to guidance, estimates and narrative over 6 to 12 months

Conclusion: the next six to twelve months offer modest, margin-led EPS upgrades and a probable guidance raise, offset by likely cuts to cash consensus; a restart of the positive narrative therefore depends on the FY2030 number, the buyback and the absence of an order collapse, not on estimates being too low.

The set-up for the next twelve months favours a guidance raise but leaves little room for EPS upgrades. The FY2027 guide is likely to be set below our numbers (topic 4), and the habitual raise points are May and August 2027. FY2027 revisions are still positive but have slowed to a crawl: EPS rose 1% in the last month, after 47% over twelve months. Brokers are trimming target prices for the sector de-rating while their estimates edge up. Buy ratings make up 63%, and the two sell ratings (Barclays and Rothschild & Co Redburn) are calls on valuation and the capital cycle, not on earnings. Per-broker FY2028 EPS ranges from €6.56 to €9.50, and the dispersion comes from margins, not revenue.

We expect EPS consensus to edge up and free cash flow consensus to be cut; the cash cut is the most probable revision we forecast. Margins should lift FY2027 to FY2028 EPS consensus modestly, while currency and wind trim revenue consensus. Free cash flow consensus should fall as the company's cash guide and the working-capital unwind come into view; we put a 70% probability on that cut. The FY2030 target on 11 November will set FY2029 to FY2030 consensus. Revision breadth should turn briefly positive after 11 November and stall in February 2027, when the first year-on-year order comparison tests the "peak orders" story. Breadth should then stay net positive on EPS and net negative on cash and target prices, so a positive composite signal will mask deterioration in its components.

The narrative knows the right things in the wrong order: the favourable half of the gap is the multiple, and the unfavourable half is cash. The market over-knows and over-prices the order peak and competitor capacity, whose earnings effect is three years away; Morgan Stanley's reverse discounted-cash-flow analysis implies a terminal margin beyond 2035 of 8.5%, below the FY2026 margin. The market knows but under-prices the normalisation of cash: every broker describes it, but none has it in FY2027 to FY2028 numbers, and the €28.1bn prepayment pool is a quarter larger than the pool any published estimate uses. The market does not yet know four things: the royalty's stop date (a two-outcome input), the SG 14 offshore question, the mid-FY2027 restatement to discontinued operations, and the 24 December US fence rule as an extender of high grid pricing.
