A restart of the positive narrative depends less on estimates than on three events. Over 6 to 12 months, the scope for estimate-driven upgrades is modest and margin-led, while the scope for cash-driven cuts is real. The three events are a FY2030 target of 20% or more with a credible bridge, a buyback of €3bn a year, and two more quarters in which earnings rise about 40% and orders do not collapse. A sale price for Transformation of Industry in mid-2027 would be a further, novel step.

The cash line, not EPS, is where the surprise sits over the next six to twelve months.

Where we differ from the market: the EPS upgrade cycle for FY2027 to FY2028 is largely done, and the surprise sits in cash. The sell-side expects 11 November to be a positive catalyst (Morgan Stanley: "new targets can accelerate the consensus upgrade cycle"). We think the EPS upgrade cycle for FY2027 to FY2028 is largely done, since our own estimates are at the median, and we think the FY2030 target will be set at the market's bar rather than above it. One caution applies to our own cash view. The company-compiled consensus of 4 November shows FY2027 pre-tax free cash flow of €5.5bn, far below FactSet's €6.8bn after-tax figure and below our €7.4bn pre-tax. Either the definitions differ, or part of the sell-side has already cut its cash forecasts. If part of the sell-side has already cut, the cash bar is lower than we assumed and the narrative downside from cash is smaller. The December annual report and the Q1 cash print will settle the question.

Counter-case: expectations are crowded. Buy-side expectations run above the sell-side's, and about 70% of surveyed investors own the stock. The stock closed flat on a very strong Q3 because guidance was not upgraded. A FY2030 target of exactly 20% with a cautious cash guide could be "in line and sold".

What would change our view: a FY2027 margin guide above 15%, which would lift FY2027 consensus by 3% to 5% at once; a FY2030 target above 22%, which would force us to revisit our FY2029 to FY2030 pricing assumption; or a pre-tax cash guide below €6bn, which would cut cash consensus at once.

Score: 60, set by the Rater. Guidance, which counts most, is more likely raised than cut on FY2027 (60% for at least one raise by August 2027 against 12% for a cut), but consensus EPS is at the memo's numbers and expected to drift up only 2-5%, about 0.2-0.3 times the 13% revenue growth rate (around the 55th to 60th percentile on the illustration), while FCF consensus is likely cut 10-15% and the narrative restart depends on the FY2030 target and buyback on 11 November. Recent revisions (+3%/+10%, 70th/84th percentiles) are momentum, not scope; coherent with the group's 58 and placed just above Teqnion because the guidance raise is likelier.

#8Current momentum: guidance, estimates, narrative, technicals, and peers

Conclusion: momentum is strongly positive in guidance and estimates and strongly negative in narrative and price, for the company and for its whole cohort, and the divergence is the set-up for the case rather than a warning about earnings.

Guidance momentum is positive but decelerating. Management raised guidance twice in FY2026 and narrowed it to the upper end at Q3. Pre-close commentary is confident about the structure of the business and cautious about the next quarter: Q4 seasonality, gas orders that will not repeat every quarter, and grid pricing that is plateauing.

Estimate momentum is rated A, but the composite rating hides weaker components. FY2027 EPS and EBITDA revisions have run far ahead of sales revisions, so the upgrades are margin-led. The mean target price has fallen 3% and 2% over the shorter periods despite a 10% rise over the longer one. The sell-side is therefore holding its numbers and lowering its multiples.

Narrative momentum is negative, while positioning is still long. The story moved from "turnaround" (2024 to 2025) to "AI-power compounder" (to mid-2026) to "peak orders and what the 2030 target will say" (since August), while the fundamentals improved. Positioning is still long (63% buy ratings; 79% overweight in Refinitiv's data; 70% ownership among surveyed investors), which leaves room for capitulation.

Technical momentum is rated D, but the price action is a sharp correction within a longer uptrend, not a completed downtrend. The price of €118.68 is 23% below the 200-day average (€154) and well below the 50-day average (€143). Relative strength is in the 17th percentile of the universe, and the share price is down 32% over six months and up 15% over twelve. The 200-day average has risen in each of the last twelve months. The 52-week low is about €100.

The whole sector has de-rated, and Siemens Energy is the cohort's leveraged expression. All 16 stocks in the dashboard's electrical equipment sector carry a technical momentum rating of D or F and a thematic momentum rating of D. Within the sector, the contracted-margin names have de-rated to the bottom third of their own multiple histories while keeping earnings momentum of A or B, and the diffuse, short-cycle compounders sit in the top quartile of their histories (second chart below). GE Vernova, the sector's bellwether, beat and raised again in October (gas pricing +50% year on year; a Power EBITDA margin of 21.4%; slots sold into 2032), and analysts saw "questions as well as answers" for Siemens Energy in the read-across, because of the pricing gap. Siemens Energy's six-month fall was about twice the basket's.

Momentum is split along the line that defines the whole case. Fundamental momentum (guidance and estimates) is positive, market momentum (narrative and technicals) is negative, and the two have diverged for six months. Among the peers, only Legrand and NKT show a wider gap between the two.

Where we differ from the market: the share price is telling us about the regime, not about earnings. The market reads the technical and narrative momentum as information about earnings. We read it as information about the market regime and the cohort, with a company overlay (peak orders, the GE Vernova pricing gap, wind). The divergence between an A on estimates and a D on price is the precondition for the return construction in topic 12, in which earnings carry the return without a re-rating.

Counter-case: divergences can resolve either way. In long-cycle capital goods, share prices have historically peaked with order growth, not with earnings, and have de-rated 12 to 24 months before the earnings peak. Both of our environment tilts (Momentum Underweight and Fragility Double Underweight) point against the stock.

What would change our view: a reclaim of the 50-day average after 11 November, or a break below €100; a turn in the sector's momentum ratings; or GE Vernova's Q4 results in late January, the bellwether for order momentum.

Score: 55, set by the Rater. One measure in the top fifth and one in the bottom fifth gives C (mixed): guidance raised twice and FY2027 EPS +3%/+11% over three and six months (about 0.2 and 0.8 times revenue growth) against a price 23% below its 200-day average, falling target prices, a narrative turned to peak orders and a cohort with every technical rating D or F. Placed low in the band because the market parts are strongly negative, but not moved to D because guidance and estimates are genuinely positive and the 200-day average is still rising.

#9Riskiness and simplicity of the forecasts and expectations

Conclusion: the forecasts are unusually low-risk and trackable on earnings, medium-risk and lagging on cash, and the share price carries high, mostly cohort-driven risk, with a short list of discrete negative tails whose combined odds are about one in three.

The case is simple at the core and complicated at the edges. The core is one driver that holds if five observable conditions hold (figure below). Two facts support the no-cancellation condition: regulated utilities hold 76% of the turbine backlog and data-centre developers 24%, and reservation fees are non-refundable. Indexation supports the no-overrun condition. Around the core sit three portfolio discontinuities (the Transformation of Industry deconsolidation, the India consolidation and the royalty removal), a restatement to discontinued operations in mid-FY2027, four bases of EPS and three of free cash flow, and a cash line for which the company gives no bridge. Our environment tilt (Fragility Double Underweight) penalises exactly this multi-part structure.

The thesis needs no new demand, pricing or competitive wins; it needs the factory and the foundry to keep their dates and wind not to break. Five strengths are still to be acquired:

  • The large-turbine ramp: castings are booked through the late 2020s at Howmet, new casting capacity arrives only in late 2028, and Yingliu's new furnaces arrive by 2027.
  • Electrical steel and bushing supply: transformer lead times exceed 100 weeks, and Swiss bushing lead times are 68 weeks.
  • Skilled labour: transmission has five retirees for every new entrant.
  • Wind at a 3% to 4% margin in FY2028: wind has had one profitable quarter since FY2022, and Vestas took four years to move from -11% to 8% to 9%.
  • Parallel execution of the 2027 agenda.

The tails over 18 months are discrete and none threatens solvency, but together they threaten EPS by 5% to 20% and cash by more. The table sizes each tail. The largest, a systemic SG 14 offshore finding or a top-up of onshore provisions, would cost €1bn to €2bn, mostly in special items and cash, plus 0.5 to 1 point of run-rate margin. Ørsted's report of 5 November is reassuring: the thermal cause can be mitigated through regular maintenance, the blade damage is "expected to be a single event", and a repair plan is agreed. The failure mechanism, however, is undisclosed.

Profit is trackable every quarter, cash only with a lag, and the post-2028 margin not at all. Public disclosure (segment margins, unit counts, commitments, conversions) tracks the profit path each quarter. The contract-liability balance tracks the cash path, but only with a two- to three-quarter lag. Nothing disclosed tracks the post-2028 margin, because backlog price per GW, reservation-fee cash and escalation formulas are all undisclosed. The sudden risks are wind (the company lost €7bn of market value in a day in June 2023) and sentiment (a GE Vernova miss, a hyperscaler capex cut, a placement of Siemens AG's 10% stake, or a US 10-year yield above 5%). The slow risks are orders and cash.

Sector precedents show three patterns: share prices peak with orders, prepayments become a false friend, and pricing cycles end through new capacity. Long-cycle capital goods shares peak with order growth, not with earnings, and de-rate 12 to 24 months before the earnings peak; Siemens Energy's share price fits that pattern exactly. Prepayments can mislead: at GE Power (2017 to 2019), book-to-bill fell below 1, progress collections were worked off and billions of working capital flowed out while reported profit fell more slowly, and Vestas' contract assets built up before its 2024 write-down. Pricing cycles end through new capacity, with a lag: high-voltage substation prices fell by up to 20% in 2010 to 2013, and the 2016 to 2020 gas downturn halved GE Power's margin. Wind turnarounds take longer than planned ("worser, odder, longer"). For the share price, these precedents imply a fair trough zone of about €78 to €95 (the ten-year crash band applied to cut estimates), which, after the fall already taken, is 20% to 35% below today's price.

The riskiness of the forecasts is low; the riskiness of the expectations attached to them is high.

The ranges of outcomes show the contrast between forecast risk and expectation risk. The range is narrow for EBITA (±7% in FY2027), wide for cash (±27%) and far wider for the share price (-35% to +65%), because about two-thirds of the multiple's moves are driven by the industry.

Where we differ from the market: the market prices sentiment risk as if it were fundamental risk. The market treats the stock as a high-beta proxy for AI power and prices sentiment risk as if it were fundamental risk to FY2027 to FY2028. We see the fundamental risk to earnings as modest and concentrated, the cash risk as larger than consensus holds, and the share-price risk as high but mostly driven by the cohort.

Counter-case: concentration cuts both ways. One factor carries the profit, and the company's history cannot calibrate the margin half of that factor, because the best pre-2026 margin was 6%. When that single variable turns, it turns with prices falling on top of volume.

What would change our view: a failure of any of the five core conditions in a quarterly print, a working-capital outflow above €1bn, or a second SG 14 finding.

Score: 52, set by the Rater. The earnings range is narrow (FY2027 EBITA about +/-7%, EPS about +/-8%, net cash, contracted drivers trackable quarterly), but the case is not simple: three portfolio discontinuities, a mid-FY2027 restatement, several bases of EPS and cash, a cash cone of +/-27% trackable only with a lag, discrete sudden tails (a systemic SG 14 offshore finding, a turbine-ramp slip, data-centre deferrals; combined about one in three) and a 1.5-beta, cohort-driven share price in a long-cycle sector that historically de-rates with orders. It sits just below NKT, which shares the prepayment and ramp profile without the wind tail, and between the risk groups' 50 and 68.

#10Where the stock is in its lifecycle

Conclusion: the stock is Stalling on price and narrative while the earnings thesis is still Reinforcing, and 11 November is the event most likely to decide whether the stall resolves upward (with a company-driven multiple again) or persists as a cohort-driven de-rating.

The dashboard's rule classifies the stock as Stalling, and the share-price and narrative evidence supports that label. The evidence is a 38% fall from the high, technical momentum rated D, a cohort de-rating, a narrative that has turned to "peak orders", and target prices falling while estimates rise. The fundamental evidence, by contrast, shows a thesis that is still broadening and reinforcing: earnings momentum rated A, guidance raised twice this year, segment margins at the FY2028 targets two years early, portfolio simplification under way, capital returns stepping up, and a FY2030 framework about to be set.

Our reading: the earnings thesis is in the Reinforcing phase, the share price is in the Stalling phase, and the order cycle separates the two. The market is pricing the FY2029-and-beyond part of the story (the order peak, competitor capacity, the prepayment reversal) before the FY2027 to FY2028 part has been reported. In this sector, that gap is what a late-upcycle conversion story has historically looked like: "the first half of a one-to-two-year holding in the paused-conversion cohort is the cleaner half". The stall is therefore more likely to resolve by earnings catching up with the price than by the price collapsing to the earnings, unless the cycle risk arrives early, with orders falling below revenue in FY2027 rather than in FY2028 to FY2029.

A FY2030 target of 20% or more with a €3bn-a-year buyback on 11 November is the one near-term event that could move the stock to Turning Up. That combination could make the multiple company-driven again, as it was in October 2025, when the basket explained only 19% of the stock's moves (an R-squared of 19%). Two further triggers would be two quarters of earnings growth of about 40% with orders flat rather than collapsing, and a Transformation of Industry signing at €11bn to €13bn with the proceeds returned (mid-2027).

Four events would move the stock to Collapsing: a systemic wind finding; a gas book-to-bill below 1.0 in FY2027 together with a working-capital outflow; a break in AI financing that defers data-centre deliveries; or a FY2030 target below 20% with a cautious cash guide, which a crowded holder base would read as the end of the upgrade cycle.

↑ To Turning Up
FY2030 target 20%+ with a €3bn-a-year buyback; two quarters of ~40% earnings growth with flat orders; a Transformation of Industry signing at €11bn to €13bn
↓ To Collapsing
A systemic wind finding; gas book-to-bill below 1.0 with a cash outflow; an AI-financing break; a sub-20% FY2030 target with a cautious cash guide

Where we differ from the market: we see mid-conversion, not late cycle. Judging by the multiple, the market's lifecycle reading is "late-cycle, peak earnings in sight". Our reading is "mid-conversion": the order peak and the earnings peak are two to three years apart, and the cash peak is already behind us.

Score: 55, set by the Rater. The computed Stalling is right for price and narrative (38% off the high, technical D, peak-orders narrative, falling targets) while the earnings thesis is mid-to-late Reinforcing, with consensus already at the memo's FY2027-28 EPS, the cash peak behind and the order peak probably now. That is late Reinforcing with signs of stalling and a multiple low in its range, more attractive than a pure stall because earnings keep rising 40% and 28% and 11 November could re-start it, but below Nexans because the order cycle is turning.

#11The fair multiple

Conclusion: we agree with the guideline fair multiple of about 15.5x, the 40th percentile, as the right central value for a Stalling stock with predictable earnings, an uncertain cash line and concentrated drivers; the fair range is 13x to 18x and the trough is 11x.

The guideline fair multiple is 15.47x two-year-forward earnings, the 40th percentile of the stock's own ten-year range, and the model's return calculation uses it. The Phases framework sets that guideline for a Stalling stock. The stock's own range runs from 11.2x at the 10th percentile ("crash") through 14.8x at the 35th ("conservative"), 16.8x at the median ("prudent") and 20.7x at the 75th ("defendable") to 25.1x at the 90th ("mania").

Three readings of today's multiple differ by basis and date, and we use 14.4x to 15.2x. The Phases page (6 November) shows the multiple "now" at 17.2x, with the guideline 10% below it. The dashboard (24 October) shows 14.4x on 24-month-forward consensus EPS of €8.22 at €118.68, and the model shows 15.2x on its own forward EPS. The 17.2x reading matches the 30 September month-end reading in the valuation history (price €142.6), so it is probably the latest month-end reading carried forward rather than a 6 November price. If the shares have in fact recovered toward €140, the guideline multiple sits below the market multiple and the 18-month return in topic 12 shrinks to roughly +17%.

If the shares are back near €140
The guideline multiple sits below the market and the 18-month return in topic 12 shrinks to roughly +17%.

We judge 15.47x a fair central value for this phase, for four reasons.

  1. The history is short and contains both extremes. The "ten-year" range holds only six years of data (the stock listed in September 2020), and it contains a 2023 crisis trough (6.4x) and a 2025 to 2026 mania (27x), so its median is less anchored than a mature stock's. A 40th-percentile multiple, rather than the median, is the right discount for a forecast whose cash line and post-2028 slope are uncertain.
  2. The EPS to which the multiple applies is unusually predictable for 18 months (±8%), which argues against using the crash band.
  3. Siemens Energy belongs with the contracted-margin cohort, with a premium. The stock's drivers are concentrated and partly cyclical (scarcity rent, prepayment-funded cash). The market pays 17x to 21x for the diffuse-driver compounders (ABB 19.7x, Schneider 21.3x, Siemens 19.1x) and 10x to 15x for the contracted-margin cohort (Nexans 10.5x, Prysmian 13.9x, NKT 14.8x). Siemens Energy belongs in the second group with a premium for its service annuity and net cash, which is where 15.5x sits.
  4. A fair multiple should not assume that the discount to GE Vernova closes. The discount is about 45% on FY2028 EV/EBITA, within an 18-month range of 25% to 50%, and it is partly deserved for wind and the pricing gap.

The fair range is about 13x to 18x, and the bull case beyond it depends on the cohort, not the company. The lower bound of 13x applies if the FY2030 target disappoints and cash consensus is cut, leaving a Stalling stock with estimate cuts. The upper bound of 18x applies if 11 November makes the multiple company-driven again (a target of 20% or more and €3bn a year of buybacks) and the stock returns toward its "prudent" median. The trough is 11.2x. The two-year median of 22.5x is a bull case that needs the cohort to re-rate and the stress in AI financing to ease, and the company controls neither.

Where we differ from the market: the sell-side is already paying for the FY2030 margin. The market's multiple (14.4x) is slightly below the guideline. The sell-side's median target price of €205, 65% above the share price, implies 19x to 20x FY2028 EPS. We sit between the two: a fair multiple of 15.5x now, with a path to 17x to 18x that depends on delivery and portfolio events rather than on the sector.

Counter-case: growth of 43% and 28% could justify a higher multiple. With EPS growing 43% and 28% in the next two years and net cash of about €8bn, an argument based on the P/E-to-growth ratio would support a higher multiple, and peers with weaker growth trade at 19x to 21x. Against that, the growth is a one-time step-up from a priced backlog, and the market is right not to capitalise a step-up as if it were a compounding rate.

What would change our view: a FY2030 target of 22% or more with a pricing bridge we found credible (toward the 16.8x median); a working-capital outflow above €1bn or a wind charge (toward 13x); or a cohort re-rating as the stress in AI financing eases (toward 20x, for reasons outside the company).

Score: 60, set by the Rater. Neutral on both measures gives C. Placed in the upper half because both readings lean cheap (14.4x against a 15.47x guideline fair multiple and a 16.8x median), but not higher because a Stalling stock whose margin is partly scarcity rent and whose cash is prepayment-flattered deserves a below-median multiple, and the ten-year range is only six years with a crisis and a mania in it.

#12Total shareholder return

Conclusion: the +39% 18-month and +67% three-year returns at the guideline multiple are earnings returns, built on EPS of €6.5 and €8.4 rolling forward with the multiple roughly unchanged; the base case therefore needs no re-rating, the Gas and Grid margin judgement moves it most (about ±8% of EPS per two points of margin), and the exit multiple sets a range from roughly flat (crash band) to about double (two-year median).

At the guideline multiple of 15.47x, the model gives a total shareholder return of +39.4% to 31 December 2027 and +66.6% to 30 June 2029. The 18-month return is 32.8% annualised, for a value per share of €165.42; the three-year return is 21.1% annualised, for €197.70. The model's template splits the 18-month return into +3.8 points from dividends, -38.0 points from the multiple and +118.9 points from earnings (+6.6, -47.1 and +202.3 over three years). That split measures earnings growth against a trailing base and nets the multiple against it, so it is better read as a direction than as a decomposition.

In our own arithmetic, the 18-month return is almost entirely earnings. At the 18-month column the model values the shares at 15.47x a forward EPS of about €10.7 (€165.42 divided by 15.47), against about €7.8 of forward EPS in today's 15.2x on €118.68. The 18-month return is therefore about +37 points from forward EPS rolling from FY2027-to-FY2028 toward FY2029-to-FY2030, about +2 points from the multiple (15.2x to 15.47x), and about 2 to 4 points from dividends (€1.90 for FY2026, paid in February 2027; the template counts €3.8 of payments). At the three-year column, the forward EPS is about €12.8 (€197.70 divided by 15.47) and the multiple is unchanged, so the three-year return is also almost entirely earnings: EPS growth of 43%, 28%, 20% and 15% compounding through FY2030, plus dividends of €2.60 to €3.95 a year, with no re-rating assumed.

The return needs only that Siemens Energy does not de-rate further, not that the cohort re-rates; earnings carry the base case and the multiple sets the range. Each turn of the exit multiple is worth about €10.7 a share, or 9 points of 18-month return. At the ten-year median (16.8x), the 18-month value is about €180 (+52%). At the crash band (11.2x), it is about €120, roughly today's price before dividends. At the two-year median (22.5x), it is about €240 (+100%), the bull case that needs a change in the market regime.

Six judgements move the value most. The figures are for FY2028 unless stated; each €100m of EBITA is worth about €0.09 of EPS, or about 1.1%.

  1. Gas Services and Grid margins at 20% each in FY2028. Two points lower on both (18%, the bottom of the Capital Markets Day range) takes EBITA down €0.77bn (-8.4%) and EPS down €0.71 to €7.65 (-8.5%), worth about €11 a share at 15.47x. Two points higher (22%, the bull case) is the mirror image, with EPS of €9.07.
  2. Wind at a 3.5% margin in FY2028, with no charge. Wind at 0% takes EBITA down €0.37bn and EPS down €0.34 (-4%). A €1bn systemic charge on top would cost about €0.92 of reported EPS as a special item and €1bn of cash, and would probably de-rate the stock toward 13x on the quality question (about -15% on the price).
  3. Orders and the prepayment loop. If FY2027 orders are about €50bn (Morgan Stanley's bear case) instead of our €58bn, working capital swings €2bn to €3bn against the company, FY2028 free cash flow falls from €5.2bn to €2bn to €3bn, net cash falls to about €2bn after India, buybacks are cut to €1bn to €2bn (EPS -1% to -2%), and the multiple moves toward the crash band. At 11.2x on about €10.3 of forward EPS, the price would be about €115, flat on today, so the cyclical bear case costs the return but not the capital, unless estimates are also cut.
  4. The large-turbine ramp (FY2027). A two-quarter slip defers €0.3bn to €0.4bn of FY2027 EBITA (-4% to -5%), taking FY2027 EPS to about €6.2 instead of €6.54; the revenue is recovered in FY2028.
  5. The royalty. A saving of €400m instead of €250m in FY2028 adds €0.14 to EPS (+1.6%); no saving until FY2030 subtracts €0.23 (-2.7%). The royalty is small in EPS terms, but it matters more for the credibility of a FY2030 target of 20% or more.
  6. Currency. A 10% move in the euro-dollar rate is worth about 3% of reported revenue and, because profit translates with revenue, about 2% to 3% of EPS (€0.17 to €0.25), with no effect on the margin.

Three portfolio items matter less. The buyback pace (€3bn against €2bn a year) is worth about 1% of FY2028 EPS. The India consolidation is close to EPS-neutral after minorities. The Transformation of Industry deconsolidation lowers EPS by 1% to 2% if the proceeds are used for buybacks and by about 5% if they are held as cash, while it lifts the reported margin.

Where we differ from the market: we would not pay now for the re-rating in the sell-side's targets. The sell-side's median target price (€205) is about 24% above the model's 18-month value and implies a re-rating to 19x to 20x FY2028 EPS. We would not pay for that re-rating in a Stalling phase. We would take the earnings return and treat the multiple as a free option in both directions.

Counter-case: the timing could slip. The 18-month column ends on 31 December 2027. If the de-rating deepens into the February 2027 order comparison and the FY2028 cash unwind, the earnings return arrives later than the model shows.

What would change our view: the same five readings that recur throughout this memo: the 11 November framework; the Q1 FY2027 turbine count and gas orders; the Taiwan finding; the contract-liability balance; and the euro-dollar rate.

Score: 90, set by the Rater. About +39% maps to about 91 and is almost entirely earnings, with no re-rating needed and the three-year check strongly supportive; placed at the floor of A because the memo's mean sits below its mode (discrete negative tails of about one in three), the crash-band multiple gives roughly flat, and if the shares have recovered toward the 17.2x Phases reading the 18-month return shrinks to about +17%.

#13Summary conclusion

Siemens Energy is a late-upcycle backlog-conversion story with a strong corporate-change overlay, priced as if the cycle had already turned. The return at the guideline multiple (+39% to December 2027, +67% to June 2029) is an earnings return that needs no re-rating, and the exit multiple sets a range from roughly flat to roughly double.

The engine: contractual and observable

A €162bn backlog at repriced margins; capacity already being installed; segment margins already at the FY2028 targets; and a management team that guides low and raises on evidence. Our FY2027 to FY2028 EPS of €6.5 and €8.4 sits at consensus, with a range of about ±8% and the most likely outcome above the base.

What makes the case less than clean

A €28.1bn prepayment pool that has stopped adding cash and will give some back from FY2028, so free cash flow falls while profit rises and our cash sits €1bn a year below consensus; a FY2030 margin target about to be set at 20% or above against our 18.4%; wind inside the perimeter, with an offshore platform under investigation; a 2027 calendar that stacks a carve-out, a rebrand, an acquisition and two capacity ramps; and a multiple that has become a 1.5-beta expression of an AI-power cohort in a risk-off regime.

Over the next twelve months, the skew is favourable on earnings and on the multiple. Guidance will probably be raised, estimates are not too high, and the peak-orders risk that drove the de-rating does not reach the income statement until FY2030. Meanwhile, the crash-band multiple applied to end-2027 forward earnings gives roughly today's price.

Over 18 months to three years, the skew is less favourable on cash and on the FY2029 to FY2030 slope, and that is where our view and market expectations will collide.

11 November decides which half of the range the stock enters. A FY2030 target of 20% or more, a €3bn-a-year buyback and a clear royalty framework would make the multiple company-driven again. A cautious cash guide delivered to a crowded holder base would extend the stall.

Thesis's Change Forces' Strength: 90, set by the Rater. Both input forces are strong and funded (contracted gas and grid demand with dated regulation at 87; a broad internal reset in pricing discipline, capacity, portfolio and capital returns at 84) and they are already turning into sharply better profits, with forecast EPS growth of about 25% a year (A, 94) and consensus growth at the 91st percentile; stronger than Richard's Arteche 80 because both sides are top-decile and the step-up is in a contracted backlog, held at 90 rather than above by wind and the turning order cycle that soften FY2029-30.

Foundations' Robustness: 68, set by the Rater. Gas and grid have durable, barrier-protected foundations (oligopoly, service annuity, prequalification, net cash) and the delivery record since FY2024 is excellent (topic 4 at 80), but quality sits at 70 because a quarter of revenue is weak-franchise wind, half of today's pricing is dated scarcity rent, returns are prepayment-flattered and the last gas downcycle took margins from 16% to 5%, so the business is less stable and predictable than Richard's 80s (Arteche, CVS Group) and above his Judges Scientific 60.

Setups' Fit/Crispness: 78, set by the Rater. In substance this is a Demand-driven EPS step-up: the demand, the booked price, the capacity being installed and the delivery (segment margins at FY2028 targets two years early) are all present, which is the textbook core Richard scored 95 for Arteche; the fit is blurred by current problems in the business (an offshore wind platform under investigation inside the perimeter, three portfolio discontinuities and a restatement layering a corporate-change overlay on the step-up), while the Stalling price and peak-orders concern are timing and price and are not counted here.

Case Riskiness: 52, set by the Rater. The operating case is narrow and trackable on earnings and has net cash, and the multiple is low in its range rather than high (unlike Richard's Arteche 60), but the case is not simple (several segments, perimeter changes, bases of profit and cash, a lagging cash line), it carries discrete sudden tails with combined odds of about one in three and a 1.5-beta, theme-driven share price in a hostile regime, so it sits at the typical level, matching topic 9's 52.

End notes

Conventions. The fiscal year ends on 30 September. Unless stated otherwise, "margin" means profit before special items (the company's key performance indicator, which FactSet's consensus "EBIT" tracks), "EPS" means adjusted EPS, and the forecasts are the Financial Analyst's model (update 2). Money is in euros. The share price used throughout is €118.68 (25 October 2026), the price in the model.

Terms. Contract liabilities are customer prepayments and advance billings. "Phases" is the lifecycle framework (Turning up, Reinforcing, Stalling, Collapsing) whose guideline sets the fair multiple for each phase. The ten-year multiple bands ("crash", "conservative", "prudent", "defendable", "mania") are the stock's own 10th, 35th, 50th, 75th and 90th percentiles. Momentum Underweight and Fragility Double Underweight are our environment tilts. Abbreviations: CMD, Capital Markets Day; HVDC, high-voltage direct current; SF6, sulphur hexafluoride; ROIC, return on invested capital; FCF, free cash flow; TSR, total shareholder return; AGM, annual general meeting; pp, percentage points.

Ranges. The "cones" in the Rater's score notes are the ranges of outcomes described in the text (for example, FY2027 EBITA ±7%, free cash flow ±27%, share price -35% to +65% over 18 months).

Charts drawn for this page (in visuals/drawn/ and visuals/drawn-copy-editor/) take their figures from the memo. Default charts and tables are from FactSet, the Master Dashboard and the one-page summary of the Financial Analyst's model; each carries its own source note. Consensus estimates are shown by named financial year.

Free cash flow: the profit-against-cash chart uses the base-case table's equity free cash flow; elsewhere the memo cites free cash flow after tax and leases and pre-tax free cash flow, which are different bases.

The financials table of ten years of history then consensus is not shown, because the annual history and FactSet consensus tables carry the same figures.

How to read this page

Every rating of this stock on one page: the Rater's 1-100 number, its letter and the Rater's own reason (at most three sentences, taken from the ratings file; nothing newly written). The number is the company's approximate standing in the Universe of about 1,300 listed European companies (90 = better than about 9 in 10; 50 = typical). A letter follows its item's rule: rank among the stocks scored (A the top 10%; B+ and B the next 15%; C+, C and C- the next 25%; D the next 25%; F the bottom 25%); or Richard's cut-offs on the measure for the four numerical topics (forecast financials, current momentum, the fair multiple, total shareholder return). On the change-forces items the number carries a sign (50 = neither positive nor negative) and the letter is the rank, so read the two together. "9th of 30 stocks scored" is the stock's place on that item. A dashed badge is provisional (fewer than 30 stocks scored).
